# Part A: What happened to CBA? (in class)

::: {.callout-important title="Read this before the workshop"}
This task is released a week ahead. Organise your group and do the digging beforehand. You get 20 minutes in class to finalise before presenting.
:::

## The puzzle

In the lecture we looked at the majors' liquidity ratios. One number stands out.

| | CBA | NAB | ANZ | Westpac |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Financial year ends | 30 Jun | 30 Sep | 30 Sep | 30 Sep |
| NSFR, FY2023 | 124% | 116% | 116.4% | 115% |
| NSFR, FY2025 | 115% | 116% | 114.6% | 113% |
| Change | **-9** | 0 | -1.8 | -2 |
| LCR, FY2023 | 131% | 140% | 132.9% | 134% |
| LCR, FY2025 | 130% | 135% | 132.1% | 137% |

CBA lost **nine percentage points** of NSFR in two years. Over the same period its LCR moved by one point, and NAB's NSFR did not move at all.

Your job is to work out **why**, and to tell the class whether it matters.

## What you'll do

In your assignment group (the same group as the group assignment; if you have not formed one, this is your reminder), prepare a **5-minute pitch** answering four questions.

::: {.callout-warning title="The four questions"}
1. **What is the NSFR measuring that the LCR is not?** One slide. If you cannot answer this, the rest will not make sense.
2. **Decompose the fall.** Did available stable funding shrink, did required stable funding grow, or both? Find the actual numbers in CBA's Pillar 3 disclosures for FY2023 and FY2025 and show them.
3. **Explain it.** Give your best-supported account of what drove the change, with evidence. State what you could not verify.
4. **Does it matter?** Is a fall from 124% to 115% a deterioration, a normalisation, or something else? Take a position and defend it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Hypotheses worth testing"}
You are not expected to arrive at one right answer. You are expected to test candidates against evidence:

- Something happened to a large, long-dated source of funding that Australian banks had in 2023 and no longer have.
- The denominator may simply have grown. What kind of asset carries the heaviest stable funding requirement, and what has CBA been writing a lot of?
- CBA started highest of the four. Convergence towards peers is a different story from deterioration.
:::

## How to get this done: use AI

::: {.callout-tip title="AI is your research assistant, so use it well"}
You are encouraged to use ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot or similar. Some ideas:

- Ask it to locate and summarise the NSFR sections of CBA's FY2023 and FY2025 Pillar 3 disclosures.
- Have it extract a comparison table of ASF and RSF components across the two years.
- Ask it to explain unfamiliar line items, for example "what counts as an operational deposit?" or "why do residential mortgages carry a 65% RSF factor?".
- Ask it what happened to Australian bank funding between 2023 and 2025. Then verify whatever it tells you.

Two rules:

- **Verify every number.** AI hallucinates confidently, and it is especially bad at reading tables out of PDFs. Cross-check against the actual Pillar 3 document.
- **Cite your sources** on the last slide, including any AI tool used.
:::

## Where to find the data

| Source | What you'll find |
|--------|------------------|
| CBA investor centre, Pillar 3 capital disclosures | The LIQ2 table: ASF and RSF by component, both years |
| CBA Pillar 3 narrative, just before the LIQ2 table | CBA's own one-paragraph explanation of the movement |
| CBA annual reports, FY2023 and FY2025 | Balance sheet, loan growth, deposit and funding mix |
| RBA, Term Funding Facility pages and the 2024 review | Size, terms and maturity profile of pandemic-era funding |
| The other three majors' Pillar 3 reports | Your control group. Did the same thing happen to them? |

Starter links:

- [CBA Pillar 3 capital disclosures](https://www.commbank.com.au/about-us/investors/regulatory-disclosure/pillar-3-capital-disclosures.html)
- [NAB regulatory disclosures](https://www.nab.com.au/about-us/shareholder-centre/regulatory-disclosures)
- [ANZ regulatory disclosures](https://www.anz.com/shareholder/centre/reporting/regulatory-disclosure/)
- [Westpac Pillar 3](https://www.westpac.com.au/about-westpac/investor-centre/financial-information/regulatory-disclosures/)
- [RBA review of the Term Funding Facility](https://www.rba.gov.au/monetary-policy/reviews/term-funding-facility/)
- [APRA APS 330 Public Disclosure](https://www.apra.gov.au/public-disclosure-requirements-for-authorised-deposit-taking-institutions)

## On the day

- 20 minutes to finalise your slides and rehearse.
- 5 minutes per group to present, 2 minutes for questions.
- Bring a laptop, or email me your slides before class and I will project from mine.
- No slides is survivable, but they will help you a lot in 5 minutes.

## What makes a good pitch

::: {.callout-tip}
- **Numbers, not adjectives.** "ASF grew 1.2% while RSF grew 2.1%" beats "funding got worse".
- **Say what you could not find.** The disclosures do not decompose everything. Naming the gap is stronger than papering over it.
- **Use the control group.** If your explanation applies to all four banks, it cannot explain why only CBA moved nine points.
- **Take a position on question 4.** Committees do not pay for "it depends".
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common pitfalls"}
- **"Lower NSFR means the bank is in trouble."** 115% clears the 100% minimum comfortably. Carrying a very high ratio is expensive, so falling is not automatically bad.
- **"The LCR and NSFR should move together."** They answer different questions over different horizons. The whole puzzle rests on their having moved apart.
- **Reading a point-in-time NSFR as an average.** The NSFR is reported at a balance date; the LCR is a quarterly average of daily values. Do not compare them as if they were the same kind of number.
- **AI-sourced figures that were never checked.** If a number on your slide is not in a document you opened, take it off the slide.
:::

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="include-answers"}
::: {.callout-tip title="Debrief notes"}
**Question 1.** The LCR asks whether liquid assets cover 30 days of stressed outflow. The NSFR asks whether long-dated assets are matched by funding that will still be there in a year. A bank can hold an ample HQLA stock, so the LCR holds, while the *term* of its funding shortens or its asset book lengthens underneath it. That is exactly the pattern in the table.

**Question 2.** Both sides moved, and the denominator moved faster. The clearest single illustration is CBA's own commentary on the June 2025 quarter alone: ASF rose 1.2% on growth in retail and SME deposits and higher regulatory capital, while RSF rose 2.1% on growth in residential mortgages and corporate lending. That one quarter accounts for only a point of the fall, so groups must add up the movements across the whole window rather than generalise from it. The mechanism it shows is the right one: a ratio falls whenever the denominator outgrows the numerator, even with both rising.

Groups should also note the balance dates. CBA reports at 30 June and the other three at 30 September, so "FY2023" is not the same day for all four.

**Question 3.** Two forces, and good groups will separate them.

- *Asset growth.* Residential mortgages carry a 65% RSF factor and business lending 85%, so credit growth mechanically raises the stable funding requirement. CBA names residential mortgages and corporate lending as the main RSF contributors.
- *The Term Funding Facility.* Banks drew \$188 billion, about 88% of the \$213 billion available, at three-year terms during the pandemic. While outstanding it was close to perfect available stable funding. The final tranche matured on **30 June 2024**, inside this window, and replacing it with deposits and shorter wholesale paper lowers ASF without touching the HQLA stock, which is why the LCR barely reacted.

What groups cannot fully verify from the disclosures is the split between the two. Credit for saying so.

**Question 4.** The strongest answer is that this is mostly **normalisation**, with two supports. CBA entered the period as the highest of the four and is now in line with peers, so the gap closed rather than a problem opening. And an NSFR far above 100% is costly: it means funding long assets with expensive long money. The counter-argument worth crediting is that the buffer above the minimum is now thinner at a time when regulators are revisiting funding assumptions after 2023, so there is less room before the ratio binds.

**On the control group.** NAB was flat, ANZ fell 1.8 points and Westpac 2. Any explanation resting only on system-wide events, the TFF included, has to also explain why CBA moved five times as far. The most likely reconciliation is CBA's starting level plus its mortgage share, not a different shock.
:::
:::

## Q1: Compute an LCR

Kestrel Bank reports the following (\$ millions).

| Liquid assets | \$ | Tier | Funding | \$ | Run-off |
|---|--:|---|---|--:|--:|
| Cash and central bank reserves | 20 | Level 1 | Stable retail deposits | 200 | 3% |
| Government bonds | 40 | Level 1 | Less stable retail deposits | 100 | 10% |
| Covered bonds | 60 | Level 2A | Operational deposits, corporates | 80 | 25% |
| Corporate equities | 20 | Level 2B | Non-operational funding, financials | 50 | 100% |

Cash inflows over the next 30 days are \$11 million. Level 2A takes a 15% haircut, Level 2B a 50% haircut.

(a) Compute the stock of HQLA, the total net cash outflows, and the LCR. Does the bank meet the minimum?
(b) The bank buys a further \$30 million of covered bonds. What is the new LCR?
(c) Instead of (b), it buys \$30 million of government bonds. What is the new LCR? Explain why (b) and (c) differ.

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="include-answers"}
::: {.callout-tip title="Example answer"}
(a) Level 1 is $20+40 = 60$, which needs no haircut.

After haircuts, Level 2A is $60 \times 0.85 = 51$ and Level 2B is $20 \times 0.50 = 10$, so $61$ of Level 2 is available.

Level 2 may not exceed 40% of HQLA, which means Level 1 must be at least 60% of it. So the most Level 2 that can count is
$$\tfrac{60}{0.6} - 60 = \tfrac{2}{3}\times 60 = 40$$
Only 40 of the 61 available counts, and $\text{HQLA} = 60 + 40 = \mathbf{100}$.

Outflows are $200(0.03) + 100(0.10) + 80(0.25) + 50(1.00) = 6 + 10 + 20 + 50 = 86$.

Inflows are capped at 75% of outflows, that is $64.5$. Actual inflows of 11 are below the cap, so all 11 count:
$$\text{Net cash outflows} = 86 - 11 = 75$$
$$\text{LCR} = \frac{100}{75} = \mathbf{133.3\%} \ge 100\%$$
The bank passes.

(b) Level 2A after haircut becomes $90 \times 0.85 = 76.5$, so $86.5$ of Level 2 is available. The cap is still $\tfrac{2}{3} \times 60 = 40$, because Level 1 has not changed. HQLA stays at 100 and the LCR stays at **133.3%**. The purchase bought no liquidity at all for regulatory purposes.

(c) Level 1 becomes $60 + 30 = 90$, so the cap rises to $\tfrac{2}{3} \times 90 = 60$. Now 60 of the 61 available Level 2 counts, and $\text{HQLA} = 90 + 60 = 150$:
$$\text{LCR} = \frac{150}{75} = \mathbf{200\%}$$

The difference is that the cap is expressed as a share of HQLA, so it scales with Level 1. Buying Level 1 assets raises the numerator **and** lifts the ceiling on how much Level 2 may count. Buying more Level 2 when the cap already binds does neither. This is why banks facing a binding cap buy government paper rather than covered bonds.
:::
:::

## Q2: Compute an NSFR

Kestrel Bank's funding and assets are as follows (\$ millions). Use the ASF and RSF factors from the lecture.

::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="50%"}
| Funding | \$ | ASF |
|---|--:|--:|
| Capital | 50 | 100% |
| Stable retail deposits | 150 | 95% |
| Less stable retail deposits | 80 | 90% |
| Corporate funding under 1 year | 60 | 50% |
| Financial institution funding under 6 months | 200 | 0% |
::::
:::: {.column width="50%"}
| Assets | \$ | RSF |
|---|--:|--:|
| Cash and central bank reserves | 20 | 0% |
| Level 1 HQLA | 40 | 5% |
| Residential mortgages | 300 | 65% |
| Other performing loans over 1 year | 150 | 85% |
| Undrawn committed facilities | 60 | 5% |
::::
:::

(a) Compute available stable funding, required stable funding, and the NSFR. Does the bank pass?
(b) The bank plans to replace some of its short-term financial institution funding with debt maturing in more than one year. How much must it convert to reach an NSFR of exactly 100%?
(c) Kestrel passed the LCR in Q1 but not the NSFR here. Explain in two sentences how that is possible.

::: {.content-hidden unless-meta="include-answers"}
::: {.callout-tip title="Example answer"}
(a) Available stable funding:
$$50(1.00) + 150(0.95) + 80(0.90) + 60(0.50) + 200(0) = 50 + 142.5 + 72 + 30 + 0 = \mathbf{294.5}$$

Required stable funding:
$$20(0) + 40(0.05) + 300(0.65) + 150(0.85) + 60(0.05) = 0 + 2 + 195 + 127.5 + 3 = \mathbf{327.5}$$

$$\text{NSFR} = \frac{294.5}{327.5} = \mathbf{89.9\%} < 100\%$$

The bank **fails**. Note where the requirement comes from: the mortgage book alone accounts for 195 of the 327.5.

(b) The shortfall is $327.5 - 294.5 = 33$. Funding from financial institutions with under six months to run carries an ASF factor of 0%, and debt maturing beyond one year carries 100%, so each dollar converted adds a full dollar of ASF. The bank must convert **\$33 million**.

(c) The two ratios ask different questions over different horizons. The LCR asks whether liquid assets cover 30 days of stressed outflow, and Kestrel holds enough HQLA for that. The NSFR asks whether long-dated assets are matched by funding that will still be there in a year, and a \$300 million mortgage book funded largely by short-term financial institution money fails that test no matter how much HQLA sits alongside it.
:::
:::
